After about 16 hours on Resident Evil Requiem (with roughly 12 hours to finish the story), I came out of it genuinely impressed. The game leans heavily into a dense, oppressive atmosphere, very much in line with Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, while also delivering fast-paced, intense action similar to Resident Evil 4, especially during Leon’s segments. That balance works extremely well: you’re constantly shifting between tension and chaos, with barely any real downtime, making the whole experience highly immersive… and honestly pretty exhausting in a good way.  It’s a very stressful game from start to finish, with memorable enemies like Gideon who keep you under constant pressure. I played my first run on normal and it was already quite challenging, but it definitely makes me want to jump back in on the “demented” difficulty to unlock everything. In the end, even if it doesn’t completely reinvent the formula, Resident Evil Requiem delivers a tightly crafted, intense, and memorable experience. It’s not a game to relax with—but that’s exactly what makes it so effective.  9/10

[b] Review written by Gemini using my bullets: [/b]  After finishing my fourth run and finally securing the Platinum trophy, I’m ready to give my verdict: In my opinion, this is the weakest entry the series has seen in a long time—especially coming off the back of the incredible RE4 Remake. As a huge RE fan, I was very disappointed...  [h3] Pros: [/h3]  - Leon is back! It’s always a highlight to step back into his shoes. - Strong Start: The first part of the game in the asylum is genuinely good. It has the atmosphere and tension you expect from the franchise. - Creative Combat: Being able to pick up and use chainsaws from zombies is a great addition. - Detailed Enemies: The zombies having "personalities" based on their former lives was a nice touch for immersion.  [h3] Cons: [/h3]  Unfortunately, as soon as you leave the asylum, the game takes a massive hit in quality: - Raccoon City is a Letdown: This segment is atmospherically weak and visually boring. It’s just a gray, monotonous backdrop with zero variety.  - Compared to the polished and "round" gameplay of RE4 Remake, Leons gameplay felt clunky and uninspired most parts of the game. - Lore Breaking: It makes zero sense that zombies infected more than 20 years ago show the exact same viral traits as the fresh ones in the asylum. It completely ignores the established timeline of virus variants. - Mechanical Failures: There are far too few boss fights, and the ones that exist are poorly designed. The puzzles are almost non-existent or incredibly lazy. - Missing Features: No real New Game+, and replacing the Merchant with a boring "box" takes away a lot of the series' character. - Artificial Difficulty: Playing on "Insanity" isn't fun or rewarding like it was in RE4; here, it just feels unfair and tedious in many cases. - Missing the "Vibe": It lacks that mysterious, captivating atmosphere that made Village and RE4 so special. Due to the lack of variety in locations, the game feels strangely short.  Unfortunately I cannot recommend the game for the current price. Its not terrible, but mediocre at best. Enough to grab it for a couple of € in a few years, but definetly no must play... Hope they will get back on track with the next RE

Resident Evil Requiem is one of those entries that actually understands what makes Resident Evil work.  The atmosphere is top-tier. It leans hard into that slow, tense dread you’d expect from something like Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, but mixes in smoother combat and pacing similar to Resident Evil Village. You’re not just running and gunning—you’re constantly low on ammo, checking corners, and second-guessing every sound.  Gameplay feels balanced. Resource management actually matters again (huge plus), and enemies don’t feel like bullet sponges for no reason. There’s enough variety to keep things interesting without turning it into chaos.  Story is solid too—dark, grounded, and connected enough to the older games like Resident Evil without requiring you to know every detail of the lore.  Cons:  * A bit linear at times * Some predictable horror moments  Pros:  * Great atmosphere * Satisfying survival mechanics * Strong return to horror roots  Playtime: ~10–15 hours Worth it? Yes, especially if you liked RE7/Village.

Resident Evil 9 succeeds brilliantly where Resident Evil 6 had failed: managing to blend the Action Horror side of the franchise with its Survival Horror legacy. The dual-protagonist system works perfectly, to the point that you'll truly feel as if you're playing two separate games, both of which displaying the culmination of thirty years of fine tuning in the genre. The plot is as ludicrous as ever, but new ideas keep the game exciting (such as taking advantage of the zombies' distinct personalities to sneak around them as Grace, or using environment hazards to take down your foes as Leon), and there are some truly exceptional action set pieces, both for Grace and Leon.  A common criticism is that the initial section in the hospital is better than anything that follows (such as the post-nuclear Raccoon City). In a way that's true, but only because the hospital part is so well-made that it's hard for the rest of the game to compare. The Raccoon City sections are still a step above pretty much any action horror up to this point (with perhaps the exception of Dead Space Remake, which I have a soft spot for).  All in all this is peak Resident Evil, with great action, great scares, fun ideas and loads of fan service for the older fans such as myself.

Much as I enjoyed -- nay, had a blast -- with Resident Evil Requiem (especially during Grace's parts), and no matter how much of a Resident Evil-tard I am since 2003/4, I cannot just lie to myself and not admit that I also see how much of a rehash-mashup of all the other Resis it is, down to Leon's clothing (same old fitted top + a jacket that he'd obviously lose later on). It's like they took the good parts of all the other Resis and smacked them onto this new game and THEN used nostalgia to boast of a brand-new Resi. I intentionally decided to articulate my thoughts about it this much later from its release. Who knows, I might just be feeling burnt out from seeing it all over social media (even from obvious casuals) during its release. But now that the dust had settled, I only feel it apt to double down on my initial reaction, especially now that I've cleared a full playthrough of The Evil Within -- whose certain elements (blood pool, Blister Heads, subway suspended in the air, enemy juice/blood for upgrades), I think, are another "inspiration" for this "bold, new Resi". I guess the devs were pressured so much they couldn't conjure anything new during brainstorming. Heck, even Revelations was able to give me an ocean of new Resi stuff (see what I did there, hah). What puzzles me more is that the director for this new installment is the same as RE7's -- who was so brilliant in reviving the series after it suffered some identity crisis during Resi 6's release. This game proved to me once again that nostalgia cannot save something that is pretty mid to begin with (looking at you, DCEU). There was a lack of boss fights, Hunk was diminished to an afterthought, and the final boss was very underwhelming even my unfertilized and unborn nephew could figure out how to kill it. Half of the game (mostly Leon's parts) felt diminutive. In the words of my partner (who's also a long-time Resi player): The devs and CAPCOM themselves are pretty much already confident long-time fans would get the game, but they mostly took this route to reel in more casuals -- and they succeeded well. Now, imagine if it wasn't Leon in his full-blown daddyness who starred as the other protagonist of this game. What then?  I'm still looking forward to non-mercenary DLCs, though. And again, I really had a blast with this highly-optimized game.

Minor spoiler at the end of this review: 2/3 of the game in. An enjoyable entry for the Resident Evil series. With the RE Engine this oozes atmosphere and the presentation is absolutely top notch. The game almost lost me in the opening hotel where you're pursued by an unkillable zombie with scripted events (how I miss the unpredictable Xenomorph slalker in Alien: Isolation) but once the meat of the game starts it's hard not to get drawn in to the sneaking, puzzling and slow but satisfying combat.  Grace is a likeable character (vulnerable, living with anxiety and not-quite Clarice Starling) with the survival horror - although it's more fun to play as the gun-toting, roundhouse kicking Leon. Voice acting is top-notch and the antagonist Victor Gideon is suitably creepy.    The in-game logic is bizarre - why does a hospital have so many crates of ammo lying around (is this Darkplace Hospital?) and how exactly does infected blood allow you to create ammo or a molotov cocktail? Or fitting gems into a door window somehow magically open a door?  The zombies are excellent, shambling around, or as in the case of the blisterheads, jerking and twitching - and a well aimed shot in the right place can splatter blood all over the environment. The puzzles - really aren't - and it is just a case of methodically working your way through the environment. Even inventory juggling becomes less of an issue once the right upgrade is obtained. And for a survival horror game I seem to have an abundance of handgun bullets.    I would criticise the price, but with the production values this high it's difficult to do so. The game runs smoothly, the audio is immersive, the cutscenes flesh out the story - and don't drown you in exposition. Some of the set pieces are frankly hysterical - purely for the absurd level of gore and blood. If you ever wanted to play a horror movie - this is absolutely the game for you.  A couple of gripes. This is a case of excellently crafted atmosphere (at least up until the final act) taking precedence over decent (but not exceptional) gameplay. Having said that, it is gameplay which sticks to the RE lineage - and I kind of wish there was more to it. Secondly the game feels like it loses its way in the last third and it starts to feel a little too fan-servicey. There's the we've-been-here-before bit. There's a bit which is practically a  walking simulator, there's the run-away-from-the-invincible-(familiar)enemy bit. And there's a boss battle which was so dull I was asking myself when it would end. And unfortunately the sterile environment where the game finishes up just doesn't hold a candle to the earlier locations in the game.  RE works best as grounded survival horror against zombie hordes in derelict and decaying environments. It falls apart with hidden bases and antagonists with superhuman powers - it just becomes way too silly.   Still gets a thumbs up for the experience - but its an uneven one.   I will warn in advance, if you're an arachnophobe you may want to steel yourself.......

Resident Evil 9 doesn’t try to reinvent the series, and honestly, that’s why it works. From the first hour it’s clear Capcom finally remembered what makes RE feel like RE — tension, atmosphere, and that constant sense of “I’m not supposed to be here, but I have no choice.”  The atmosphere is easily the strongest part of the game. The town, the lighting, the weather, the sound design — everything blends into this slow-burn dread that feels closer to RE2 and RE4 than anything we’ve had recently. Combat has more weight than in Village, enemies push harder, and resource management actually matters again instead of being something you ignore after the first chapter.  It’s not perfect. Some sections drag longer than they should, and the enemy AI occasionally does something so dumb it breaks the immersion. You can also feel the pacing stretch in a few places, like Capcom wanted to hit a certain playtime target.  But overall? RE9 is a very solid entry. It’s confident, atmospheric, and knows exactly what kind of experience it wants to deliver. Not a masterpiece, not a disaster — just a damn good Resident Evil game that fans of the series will appreciate.  9/10 — a strong return to form with a few rough edges.

In general, I didn't like Resident Evil Requiem, perhaps because I had too many expectations. For me it is a 4 out of 10.  The enemies: For 85% of the game, the enemies are zombies, except for the bosses. It is true that they have a certain variety: not all of them behave the same and have different patterns. Even so, this does not add much either, since they are only "well" used in the first half of the game. The lack of other types of threats ends up weighing on them, especially in the second half. You would expect them to take advantage of more well-known enemies such as lickers, hunters, etc. Even the garm, they only appear in the motorcycle scene, which is a shame.   Setting/Gameplay: The first part of the game, set in the patient center, is clearly the most worked. Here you can feel the classic essence of Resident Evil: puzzles, tension, scarce resources and uncomfortable situations. It's where the game works best. But the further you go, the lazier it feels.  This is especially noticeable in the second part, when you arrive at Raccoon City. That it has been used more as a lure than as a really used location. On paper it sounded very good to return to such a mythical location, but in practice it adds almost nothing. It would have been very nice to be able to walk through its ruined and dusty streets solving the typical bizarre puzzle of the day. The real feeling is that you could be in any neighborhood of a large city and the experience would be very similar.There are recognizable details, but little else.   Another problem is the repetition of objectives. At various points in the game, you have to search for three objects to advance: the stones in the patient center, the sockets in the basement, and the detonator parts. When you think about it, it feels repetitive and uninspired. It gives the impression that it is only there to extend the duration of the game. And along the same lines, there are sections where the only thing you do is move forward without anything relevant happening, which breaks the rhythm.   The Ark laboratory does not improve the experience either. More than a laboratory, it looks like a boutique warehouse. This breaks the atmosphere that the nerve center of experimentation and export of BOWs should have. In addition, it is contradictory: it seems very large at first, but when you walk through it, it feels small.   Characters:  Grace: Leaving aside the fact that her boss sends her to investigate a traumatic place for her and stuff, because RE... Although it is not what she expected, she fulfills her role as an inexperienced and helpless young woman well. Even so, she is quite hypocritical. She worries about a girl turned into a monster, when seconds before she was happy to have killed another in the same situation. The difference is simply how she perceives them.   Leon: Leon's character fits what is expected of him. With his years of experience, he is practically an anti-BOW machine. This is reflected in the gameplay: he destroys everything without too much difficulty. But the plot of his "trauma" with Racoon city is very wasted.   Conclusion: The first half of the game is fine, but it concentrates practically all the interesting ideas such as zombies with personality. But a little before the middle of the game, it starts to wane, especially when you reach Raccoon City.  In short, it's a game with a good start, but it takes advantage of its strengths poorly. The filler and lack of ideas ends up weighing down the experience.

This is one of the cases I wish you could leave a review without recommending/not recommending the game because neither option would sit too well with me. But with 160k positive reviews, my vote won't change anything anyway.  As someone who has played 15 RE games (only finished 9 though), I find their current direction to be rather strange and unusual. Any franchise that is as enduring as this will have obviously gone through a lot of changes, lest it get stale. Sometimes everything might change from the ground up to the point you'd never believe the first and the latest game in the series are from the same franchise.   Not so here, but in the weirdest way possible. With every new game I feel like they try more and more and more to please everyone that has ever played this series before. It was already quite prevalent in Village, with different  chapters of the game playing out completely differently, but it's so much more in your face here. Before the first hour is over, you'll have swapped protagonists 4 times and genres at least 3. From pure horror, to pure action, to stealth, to "classic" survival horror. It's like they're trying to add a section to appeal to the fans of 1-2-3, then fans of 4-5-6, then fans of 7-8, but in my opinion it results in a very disjointed experience. There's no way everyone's just gonna love every sub-genre of horror just as much, so there's no way they'd enjoy this game consistently as much all throughout, right?  Personally, I found Leon's segments to be infinitely more fun. At least at first, but we'll get to that. Grace's segments most likely rely on you being scared to be entertained, but if you're not, it just means it's a whole lot of sitting around doing nothing, waiting for the next thing to happen. That's neither scary, nor fun, I don't do this much sitting around doing nothing in my real life, why would I pay 80 euros for that? Moreover, the more you meander about doing nothing and just observing the game doing its thing, the more you notice the seams. You start noticing the scripting, when and how your actions trigger the "next thing to happen". You start analyzing le scary woman's AI to better understand when she's gonna stop wasting your time, you start equating getting the next quest item to the next scripted appearance of her, the next scripted chase scene. The immersion is quite ruined when you see a crank or a key and immediately think "guess it's time for the next TENSE chase". Again, this probably won't apply to you if the entire time you're scared out of your wits, but unfortunately that hasn't happened to me.  Side note, but can we finally retire the absurd inventory management system from the early games? Who enjoys running back and forth from their supply stash every 10 minutes, because they can only carry a few things at a time? We're not even talking big things, it's gonna be 1 pistol, some ammo and then a bunch of small crap that even a 70 year old babushka would have enough room for in her purse. And please let's not argue that it's "more realistic" than a giant attache case, because the teleporting supply stash is far less realistic than that. It may be the most immersion breaking mechanic in the series.  If the problems ended here, I'd also end the review here saying "well Grace's part was a pain in the ass, but it was worth enduring it for Leon's". But alas, it is not so.  To semi-quote our boy Chris from RE5, more and more I find myself wondering, why do I find the design mentality of later RE games to be so strange? I knew there was a problem, I knew it annoyed me, but what was it and how was it best to define it, so I could convey my discontent to another person without them being confused? After a lot of thinking, here's the best way I can describe it.  These games, Requiem most of all, seem afraid to be games. Keep in mind, that a game by definition, does not need story or characters to exist. Tetris or Minesweeper aren't bad games because they have no story. Neither is something like Minecraft - it does have lore, but how much you care about it is up to you, and the story is one you make for yourself + the end credits if you "beat" the game. For that reason I feel like the primary directive when developing a game should be "is it gonna be fun to play?" Will the core experience, the most mundane, most regular thing you'll do in this game for the longest stretch, will be enjoyable enough?  I sincerely doubt that was the center of the developers' focus. If anything it almost feels like they got a movie production crew and told them to make a game at gunpoint. Why do I say that? Well, it's because everything in this game has to be "cinematic". From start to finish, everything has to keep being "different" and "unique", everything has to be scripted down to the most minute detail. Almost every zombie has something unique about them, which sounds cool I know, but in reality it just feels like you're always on rails, doing exactly what is wanted, exactly how it's wanted. When they want you to sneak around, they'll deprive you of bullets and give you very beefy adversaries, like the cook. So you'll sneak, you'll push the food cart, he'll react accordingly in his scripted way and you'll hide/run exactly how you're wanted to. Then you'll meet the light switch guy and well, you're still very low on ammo, so of course you'll observe and play with the lights to lure him away, exactly how they want you to. When people describe some of the older games like RE 2-3, they'll say that between limited ammo and zombies being tanky, you have to pick your fights, 'cause you can't fight them all. Well, here it feels like the game is picking the fights for you.  Leon's not immune to this phenomenon either. Sure, since he is a killing machine, they can't bother giving every enemy a personality, as there won't be enough time for those to shine. But what they'll do instead is throw in as many "events" as they can for Leon's part, so there's still next to no regular gameplay left for you to approach exactly how you want to. The gas station event, the underground parking lot event, the mortar event, the glass floor event, the mercenaries event, the devs were working tirelessly to make sure you don't get BORED to DEATH just fighting regular enemies however you wanted. I mean.... for god's sake, wasn't that always the most fun part of these games? Especially if we're talking about the action-oriented ones that Leon's campaign is supposed to be the evolution of? Sure, bosses and minibosses in 4 and 5 were usually fun, but sometimes they weren't, whereas fighting regular enemies was an absolute blast. You had the most control, the most freedom, all guns were viable in their own way so you could use whichever you preferred, it was COOL. But it's as if the moment regular gameplay lasts for longer than 15 minutes, a shareholder comes in and guns one of the dev team down for "not understanding what gamers want".  Even running is scripted. RUNNING. Lord above, help us all. As I and many others noticed, Grace runs very slowly. Now why is that? She's not old, she's not out of shape, she's in mortal danger, she should be able to run faster than she does. Well how's this for an unconfirmed theory? When the Scary Lady pops up, half the bloody time Grace immediately plummets down to the ground and starts crawling and it's all part of you holding down run and trying to get away, 'cause what else are you gonna do. Yet, the whole stumbling down and crawling sequence doesn't feel like it's slower than your regular running speed, even though it should. Why is that? Could it be they slowed Grace's overall speed down just so they could have these spots of stumbling integrated more seamlessly? Aka the entire experience made worse for yet another cinematic quirk that is almost entirely unnecessary?   I ran out of room. I like the story. Emily made me happy.

[h2] SPOILERS AHEAD [/h2]  🌸Story/Characters🌸 - Being a long time fan of Resident Evil I was so stoked to have Leon return as a playable character for the first time in a new title since RE6 and boy did they not hold back. Even with being on his practical death bed and showing his age this has got to be the BEST Leon we have gotten. He and Grace make an AMAZING duo in this game and I give so much credit to the devs for creating a character like Grace. A likeable down to earth and relatable character for us to experience true fear through. Creating a story with two characters who are completely different in all aspects made this game an absolute thrill to play through. The story kept me locked in and curious throughout as I tried to piece together who Grace was, how her background and past got her into this position and what secrets would be uncovered. All of the characters were well made and for the first time in quite a while I enjoyed the main antagonists. Gideon was nasty in an unsettling creepy Joker way and Zeno being a suave carbon copy of everyone's favorite villain was perfection.   🌸Gameplay/Combat🌸 - The gameplay and combat was definitely the highest point of the game for me. When your combat has ME roleplaying the Tyrant and chasing down every single zombie I can find to victimize them you have peak combat. Leon's combat was by far the BEST it has ever been in the franchise in my opinion. The vast array of weapon choices, satisfying parries, fun melee and BRUTAL gun finishers had me wishing there were more enemies to ruin. And even on the other side of the spectrum I loved Grace's combat as well. Stealth focused and introducing many different ways to silently and swiftly take out enemies and mini bosses was fantastic. I loved crafting acid bottles, Molotov cocktails and injectors as opposed to having her be a run and gunner like Leon. Her gameplay was the horror aspect of the game making you play carefully and methodically while his allowed you to be aggressive and bloody without a care in the world. The juxtaposition of the two was perfection. Outside of combat the rest of the gameplay was just as great. I loved the puzzles, the stealth, the crafting system and the credit system implemented for upgrades was all intriguing and done well.   🌸Graphics/Sound Design/Music🌸 - The graphics were beautiful, sharp, crisp and looked amazing even on lower settings. Capcom did an AMAZING job with the optimization and graphics of this game. Every single area and location in the game looked amazing and well designed. The ruins of Raccoon city were dusty, old and forsaken; the RPD perfectly aged from the last time we saw it in RE2; the Umbrella lab spotless, clinically clean and perfect while the care center was beautiful with each room detailed per occupation (kitchen, cells, bathrooms, offices). The sound design was immaculate especially when it came to the environment and gun/melee sounds. The tense moments were creepy and unsettling when they needed to be and kept you on edge and fearful even when nothing was happening directly to you. The OST in Resident Evil games have always been really good as well especially the main menu and final credit tracks. I especially enjoyed the remix that becomes the main menu music soon as you beat the game. Devs that change the music as well as the main menu background for different endings or new game plus is top tier design and much appreciated.    🌸Game Length/Replay Value/Difficulty🌸 - I am a "slower" gamer as I like to take my time with games and explore every corner, encounter every enemy etc and the first run took me about 12 hours to finish so about average time for a Resident Evil game. As with other games in the franchise there are multiple difficulty options with the hardest (Insanity in this title) only unlocking once you beat the game initially. Taking into account the extra difficulties, the multiple runs needed for anyone going for the Plat, and the challenges within the game to unlock cosmetics and new guns there is some replayability for those who really enjoy the game. Future dlc has also been confirmed so more content is on the way as well.   🌸Overall Rating & Final Thoughts🌸 - I loved this game. After waiting years for a new one that did not revolve around Ethan Winters this was well worth the wait. The combat, story, graphics all perfectly bundled together make this game easily in the top three for me when it comes to RE games alongside RE4R/OG and RE2R. With the amount of replayability, fun and future content planned I definitely recommend this game to RE fans and score it an easy 9/10.

Resident Evil Requiem truly feels like Capcom reclaiming its crown in survival horror. From the moment the game begins, it delivers a masterclass in atmosphere—dark corridors dripping with tension, grotesque enemy designs that keep you on edge, and a story that balances nostalgia with fresh blood.  What makes it stand out is how confidently it blends the best of both worlds: the slow-burn dread of classic Resident Evil with the adrenaline-fueled action of its modern entries. Grace Ashcroft emerges as one of the most compelling new protagonists in years, while Leon Kennedy’s return ties the game back to the franchise’s roots. The pacing, visuals, and sound design all scream polish, reminding players of Capcom’s golden era.  Yes, some critics point out repetitive objectives or predictable scares, but the overall experience is undeniably thrilling. It’s the kind of game that makes you say: Capcom is back in its prime. Fans who’ve been waiting for the series to fully embrace its legacy while pushing forward will find Requiem a triumphant return.

As a long-time fan of the entire Resident Evil series, I must say this is an absolute masterpiece - from everything to the multiple perspectives and gameplay styles to the sounds used for the guns; you will not be disappointed with this game.

As you may expect, RE Requiem is a good game. Anyone already a fan of the series will think so and new fans will enjoy it too, admittedly probably more so than old fans. This game is a mixture of RE7/8 and RE4R with superb lighting, scares, suspense, and puzzles, while also being full of plenty action and spectacle. While essentially being two games in one, for the most part, it doesn't compromise on either experience. I say for the most part because, for me, Leon's section wasn't as fun to play as Grace's sections however this is mostly due to the environment. Leon's section mainly consists of returning to an ashed post-nuclear(?) city and I just don't find it as much of an appealing location as the hospital and the obligatory lab section that every RE game consists of. This isn't necessarily to say the gameplay in those areas aren't still good however. The story overall is what'd you expect from an RE game almost to a T. However, it does feel at a certain point that they must've run out of time or something because certain characters feel woefully underutilized as if they intended more for them. If not, they were definitely wasted potential but nothing to throw a fit over if you ask me. RE Engine is a superb game engine in regards to graphics tech of course so do issues in that department. In my experience, the game is optimized just fine. It could be a tad better I feel like but anyone with a roughly PS5 equivalent PC shouldn't face any issues.  Update: Went for a replay and... while Grace's part is fine, the Raccoon City section of the game with Leon is actually really bad. The game in general also lacks much replay value, Leon Must Die is a lazy attempt at... I'm not even truly sure what they were going for with that mode. The story while fine on a first playthrough, isn't actually all that interesting like at all on my repeat playthrough. I wish I could give a more concrete reason on why this game just isn't as fun to replay as RE2R, RE3R, RE4R, RE7 (granted you can't skip cutscenes so that sucks)... I also wasn't interested in replaying RE8 either so... I suspect CAPCOM is just having some issue with making particularly interesting mainline titles that isn't a remake. It's a fine first playthrough, and maybe even a second if you play on Insanity (which I was gonna get to after beating the game one more time on Standard) but I'm having not as much fun as I've had with other RE games.

Wish there was an "Its fine" option for review.  As a game on its own merits its a good game, especially considering how most video games now a days aren't worth buying or playing.  As a Resident Evil game its very underwhelming. Its a one timer where a handful of the other RE games are worth replaying every few years.  I enjoyed the beginning section a fair bit but that only lasts about 4 or 5 hours. The rest of the game doesn't look or feel like a quality RE game but something that was rushed out the door. The aesthetics of art deco, Victorian, royalty, etc are gone the beauty of the antique puzzles isn't there either. There is no treasure hunting system.  There is no merchant.  The color palette of the entire game is white and grey. The puzzles are almost non-existent and have no depth.  The challenge is not there even on the hardest difficulty available on first play thru its just point A to point B with nothing shaking up that loop. The upgrade system for both character stats and weapons is also extremely bare bones. The combat is a huge down grade from RE4.  The mechanics are also very surface level and do not deliver anything new as you progress.  Pretty much everything novel about this entry feels gimmicky from the blood collecting/crafting system to the point system for upgrades to the enemies having part of their "personality" in tact...it feels like the devs sat at their desks for months just to try and come up with these subpar features.  Also the dual role feature feels like a missed opportunity from every angle and really isn't implemented well. Grace is the weakling, no ammo, hide and run for your life horror segment. Leon is the action literally nothing poses a threat to you segment.  It feels so disjunct.  That might all sound bad but if you have no context to go on and this is your first RE game you will probably love it.  Just know that the other titles are leaps and bounds better in every single possible category. The gameplay on both is really solid especially 8 but you will have an aneurism with how utterly f*cking stupid the story and characters are its mind numbing at times.  In conclusion 9 is fine bordering on meh.  As the months go on the hype for this title will die down and the honeymoon phase will end. Resident Evil Requiem is a great blend of two very different styles of gameplay. On one hand, it brings back classic survival horror in the spirit of Resident Evil 0, resource management, tension, and careful play. Even though you do get some weapons, playing as Grace makes you feel incredibly vulnerable. It’s genuinely scary, especially in first-person, and the game absolutely nails that feeling.  On the other hand, playing as Leon is the complete opposite... in the best way. You feel powerful, almost like a supersoldier. Throughout the game, his condition gradually deteriorates, which is a really nice touch. He gets tired faster when running, and toward the end his reload speed slows down a bit. Still, he remains a powerhouse, and using his full arsenal is just incredibly fun.  So the game gives you two very distinct experiences, and I love that. Cons: -The story isn't the strongest part of this game and neither are the villains. Also, feels like there is quite a conflict in canon regarding Ozwell E. Spencer's final moments before his death. If you have played RE5, you know what I am talking about and that it doesn't match what is being told here in Requiem. -The middle part of the game can feel slightly lacking compared to the rest. You know the term "Never judge a book by its cover"? Normally, that quote was meant to not overlook something just because it didn't look like what you want.  Well, the opposite can apply too. Just because it looked good doesn't mean that it is good. And this is the one that I saw regarding this game.  When I saw the trailers, I didn't feel hyped. Instead, I felt worried, especially when it is revealed that they were going back to Raccoon City. To me, that's where my dread regarding this game started. The shown gameplay of Grace and Leon felt... bland in their own way, and it was clear they were marketing this with fan services.  For Grace's section, it started good, but it slowly became mediocre. Scares are mostly scripted than atmospheric, outright predictable in some case. The lack of increase in power made the game boring in her sections. Worse was that, she even had three consumable items capable of instant kills, along with a magnum in the care center section. That really trivialized the survival aspect of the game if you can just removed an enemy in one hit.  Leon's section, however, it just worse. Combat was like a slog, lacking in flow. Parry had now become overpowered to the point that it is possible to block rockets. Guns felt weak as enemies don't get stun often. And often times, combat felt too damn easy. In my first playthrough, when I reached the final boss, I had about 15 healing items in the inventory. Not once was there any fight that felt like a challenge for Leon to me.  Story wise... It's bad. A whole plotline of Grace being 'The One' went nowhere. The Raccoon City Syndrome plot device that came out of the blue and resolved quite quickly due to an unknown mcguffin cure that also came out of nowhere. So much nostalgia bait all over the place. A Chloe section that ultimately was not important.  Retcons here, there, everywhere, some to the point of lore breaking... It's so bad that I want to say that this game is not canon.  Furthermore, the whole game felt lacking in many ways. Boring combat, sections that felt like a slog, and the lack of additional contents was really killing replayability of this game. So much so that I went back to play older titles midway of my first playthrough.  Overall, I definitely don't recommend this game for starters since you need a sizable knowledge of RE lore to understand the whole thing. For RE gamers... Wait for more content to drop first. But even then, thread lightly. This game does look beautiful, but it was really flawed and empty inside.  4/10

Let's get this out of the way: Resident Evil 9 - Requiem is a great addition to the franchise.  Is it the best? Not even close.  Is it worth your money? Absolutely.  The premise of the game takes place 15-or-so years in the future, long after the collapse of Umbrella, as an older, grizzled Leon S. Kennedy attempts to find answers to his own T-Virus infection, while simultaneously rescuing a young FBI agent (and key to everything), Grace, from a new threatening shadow organization that seeks the final pieces of Umbrella's research: Elpis.  Graphically, the game is beautiful, with great character models, fantastic animations and good effects.  The environments are reasonably atmospheric, albeit repetitive, with parts of the game taking place in a research hospital, orphanage and Raccoon PD, within a nuclear strike-devastated Raccoon City.  The return to Raccoon City and the eventual descent into Umbrella super-facility the Ark steal the show, with ghosts of past experiences hanging thick over your frantic pursuit of Victor and Grace. The beginning of the game is also stylish with a Condemned-vibe adding a new twist to traditional RE fare. Voice acting and sound work are acceptable.  Game play is good, albeit limited at times.  While the game gives you a decent amount of weapons, combat tactics, ranging from melee to shooting, Leon's movements are far more cumbersome than Resident Evil 4 Remake.  I'm unsure as to whether that is attributable by design to his more advanced age (he's almost 50) or if it's just an oversight.  Weapons lack punch unless fully upgraded and regular peon enemies sometimes, by sheer happenstance, seem to manifest absurd amounts of durability (4-5 headshots to put down, multiple melee strikes, 2-3 shots of heavy ammunition, etc). Of note there's a controversial vehicle section and a pronounced lack of merchants and dearth of collectibles.  Additional complaints range from a empty world in Raccoon City to short game length. All of the aforementioned are valid concerns, with the game often feels hollow or small compared to better paced/scripted predecessors. Of course, you'll also discover that the game has relatively easy bosses, whether you talk about the Super Tyrant, Plants or Victor/Nemesis.  In fact, it's of important to note that some zombie/peon fights are far harder than boss fights due to inclusion of super tanky zombies and cheesy swarming occurrences.  There are a series of horror/chase sequences with creatures like The Girl, that attempt to mimic RE 7 - Biohazard or RE 8 - Village but the chases fail to capture the dread you experienced in prior games.  All of these complaints are forgivable however, as RE 9 - Requiem is a great book end to RE 2 Remake.  We see an older, still badass, Leon continuing to face down unspeakable horrors, return to Raccoon City, and deal with the repercussions of his life-long crusade against Umbrella and its pretenders.  Gameplay, pacing and story are all good enough to make the game worthwhile, even if the title fails to hit the heady heights of RE - 8 Village or RE 4 Remake.  The lack of content does sting and that reality is only compounded by a glaring absence of multiplayer or co-op functionality.  With a more action-oriented game, RE 9 - Requiem begs either one (or both) to improve the game value proposition.  Still, you can do far worse than RE 9 - Requiem and most fans of the series will find a lot to like.  Let's just hope that Jill, Claire or Chris return for the next title.  I love Leon but it's time for someone else to get some exposure.  8.5/10. Recommended.

I had a great time with Resident Evil Requiem and it is easily a must buy for the fans of the series.  To be honest, the last Resident Evil game I played was Resident Evil 4 (the 2005 one) so I missed out on the "revival" of the series starting with 7 and the remakes. Nevertheless, I had a lot of fun with Requiem because it is a great mix of FPS horror and TPS action. Grace's sections are scary enough and the survival horror elements are almost perfect - and just when you think that "huh, okay, time for a change of pace," Leon comes and roundhouse kicks the door and provides a well-deserved break from all the tension. Also, the game looks stunning and I was genuinely impressed by all the visuals - especially the starting area on the city streets.   It has some pacing issues (sometimes I felt that either Grace's or Leon's section went on a bit longer than needed) but I guess that is part of the challenge when you want to combine a survival horror game and an action horror game. The story could have been a bit more developed as well - sure, it is Resident Evil, so you have to suspend your disbelief, but some moments were a bit too much. At the same time, of course, it IS Resident Evil - so I did appreciate the one-liners and the occasional campiness.  Overall, I had a blast and I can easily recommend Requiem to anyone who is interested in a fun mix of survival horror and action horror. The game is very fun to play and with all the unlockables, you are looking at two or maybe three walkthroughs if you want to unlock all the bonus content. While I do think that Resident Evil 4 still comfortably sits on its throne in my book, Requiem is awesome and it is one of the best in the franchise.

𝑹𝒆𝒔𝒊𝒅𝒆𝒏𝒕 𝑬𝒗𝒊𝒍 𝑹𝒆𝒒𝒖𝒊𝒆𝒎 - manages something very difficult: it blends classic survival horror with modern action without feeling like two separate games forced together. Everything revolves around the contrast between the two protagonists — Grace Ashcroft and Leon S. Kennedy — and that completely defines the experience.  𝑮𝒂𝒎𝒆𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒚 & 𝑪𝒐𝒎𝒃𝒂𝒕  This is where the game shines the most.  Grace and Leon are not just “two different skins,” but two completely different gameplay styles.  Grace = Pure Survival Horror  With Grace, the gameplay is tense, slow, and oppressive. You have limited resources, a tight inventory, weaker combat options, and the game encourages you to run more than fight. Stealth matters a lot: hiding, distracting enemies, and managing every bullet carefully feels similar to RE2 or RE7.  She is also hunted by a persistent stalker enemy, similar to Mr. X, which keeps the tension high at all times.  Leon = Action Horror  Leon is the complete opposite: shotguns, SMGs, melee finishers, parries, and aggressive combat similar to RE4. He has much more control over situations, and his sections are built for adrenaline rather than panic.  His hatchet and execution system make combat feel very satisfying and rewarding.  Combat Verdict  The idea works extremely well: Grace creates fear, Leon releases the tension. The pacing becomes very smart because of that contrast.  The only downside is that Leon’s combat sometimes lacks the brutal impact of RE4 Remake and can feel slightly more rigid.  𝑪𝒐𝒏𝒕𝒓𝒐𝒍𝒔 & 𝑴𝒐𝒗𝒆𝒎𝒆𝒏𝒕  A major strength is that you can switch between first-person and third-person for both protagonists. This gives real freedom and changes how the gameplay feels.  Grace  Her movement is intentionally heavier and more vulnerable. She doesn’t feel like an action hero—she feels scared and exposed. For some players, this may feel frustrating, but that’s exactly the point.  Leon  Leon feels faster, smoother, and more aggressive, with dodge options, melee actions, and quicker reactions. However, compared to RE4 Remake, some players may feel he is slightly stiffer.  𝑪𝒐𝒏𝒕𝒓𝒐𝒍𝒔 𝑽𝒆𝒓𝒅𝒊𝒄𝒕  Functional and smartly designed, but not perfectly polished. Grace is excellent for horror, Leon is strong for action—but Leon still doesn’t fully reach the iconic gameplay feel of RE4R.  𝑺𝒕𝒐𝒓𝒚 & 𝑪𝒐𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒏𝒖𝒊𝒕𝒚  The story is surprisingly strong.  This is not just “another outbreak.” The game is heavily connected to trauma, memory, and the legacy of Raccoon City. For Leon, returning here carries real emotional weight—it is literally where everything started for him.  Grace brings a fresh perspective: she is not a super-agent, but a vulnerable FBI analyst, and that changes the tone significantly.  The continuity is handled well, and the fan service never feels forced. Leon is not included just for nostalgia—he has a meaningful role in the narrative.  𝑴𝒖𝒔𝒊𝒄 & 𝑺𝒐𝒖𝒏𝒅  The sound design is excellent.  Grace’s sections use silence, breathing, footsteps, and environmental sounds to create anxiety. The game doesn’t rely on cheap jumpscares—it builds psychological pressure instead.  With Leon, the soundtrack becomes more cinematic and aggressive, supporting the action-heavy gameplay.  Audio is one of the main reasons first-person mode works so well here.  𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 – Grace and Leon  𝔾𝕣𝕒𝕔𝕖 𝔸𝕤𝕙𝕔𝕣𝕠𝕗𝕥  Grace is probably one of the most “human” Resident Evil protagonists in recent years.  She is not instantly a badass. She is anxious, scared, and visibly affected by what is happening around her. That makes her feel more believable. Her relationship with personal trauma and the way she grows throughout the story gives the narrative emotional weight.  Some players may think she is too vulnerable or too panicked, but that is exactly what makes her stand out.  She is not designed to be cool—she is designed to feel real.  𝕃𝕖𝕠𝕟 𝕊. 𝕂𝕖𝕟𝕟𝕖𝕕𝕪   Leon is exactly what longtime fans wanted: older, tired, but extremely capable.  He is no longer the “cool guy” from RE4—he feels like a heavier, more serious version shaped by years of trauma. Capcom handled him very well here.  His sections work because you can feel his experience. When you play as Leon, it feels like someone has entered the nightmare who already knows how horror works.  This is one of the best versions of Leon we’ve seen in years.     𝔽𝕚𝕟𝕒𝕝 𝕊𝕔𝕠𝕣𝕖: 𝟡/𝟙𝟘

*Review after 100%* After Village left a bad taste in my mouth, I really needed Resi to get back to it's routes away from the Ethan arch. And they ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ delivered. I love this game.   My first playthrough of his game, I had absolute stars in my eyes, convinced this was the best resi game to date. After finishing it - I think it's up there. But maybe Resi2R just outshines it as a complete package. At the time of review, the story is all there is. No mercenaries, no extra modes, etc.   Plot wise, it's a great; if a bit disjointed.  Without going into detail, Grace is absolutely excellent. Probably my new character in years. She's not annoying, has character development, and ends in a solid place by the end of the game.  Leon is of course,  so over it all, and just wants to go home. He's seen and done the whole rigmerole 1000 times now, and his gameplay reflect that. He rips and tears through zombies. With that said, he does reiceve some actual character development later in the game, where we see that his past experiences have done a number on him mentally.  Both of them have completely different gameplay archs, with Grace more or less where Leon was 30 years ago in Racoon city. She has a lot more horror-focused style, where you'll be conserving ammo, fighting off an unkillable foe while trying to solve puzzles. I LOVED Grace's sections. So much in fact that I didn't want to go back to the Leon sections which is just all action. If you've played Resi4R, this dymamic will be very familier. And this case, I think it actually hurts the experience. I came off Resi4, straight into Village, then into Resi9 - so by then the combat was feeling a little bit samey. But that's a personal problem. The gunplay is phenominal.   My main gripe with the game. The whole game STINKS of re-writes; and nothing in the game escapes that. Leon's whole section in Raccon city feels like it was ripped out of an older build of the game, when it was supposed to be an open-world game (yes thats what it was going to be). That section of the game really drags and feels like a waste of time. Grace's arch also feels like a little weird, where her whole backstory is put into question, then complely disregarded at the end. Also, feels like a re-write. There's a whole section 2/3's into the game where we play as a young girl, which goes absolutely nowhere, and barely ties in with anything that concludes in the story.   Basically, I think the games' plot could have had one final re-run before launching. What's there is excellent. I just wish it was a bit tighter.  Gameplay wise, it's the best in the series, bare none. I think people who enjoy the more survival horror elements of the series will put this at the very top of the series, while action lovers might put this one just under Resi4R.  I personally think it sits right next to Resi4R for me in the tier list, with only Resi2R sitting at the top. Solid 8/10. My complete tierlist: Resi6 - Resi3R - ResiVillage -Resi4 - Resi5 >Resi4R/Resi9> Resi2R.

You know you’re in for a treat when the name of the game is Leon’s magnum revolver.  Resident Evil Requiem (RE9) is the epilogue to Leon following Grace’s undertaking to solve a seemingly unrelated case with the FBI.  Does that sound odd? Well, it is.   Where Requiem is most interesting is when you’re not playing Leon. Yet, the biggest thread you pull at revolves around him. And for every moment you dig into Leon’s past (and future), all you will likely think of is “when can I play as Grace again”?  For those who don’t know, Requiem follows two protagonists. Grace Ashcroft (new character) and fan favourite Leon Kennedy. Each character has their own motivations and play style. Grace, an FBI office agent with what appears little field experience, revives the survival horror from past games, like RE2 or RE7. Leon, now tenured and a little wiser, brings the action back like John Wick, similar to RE4 or RE8.  Both characters play to their strengths (and weaknesses). Inventory, skills, and movement vary significantly. Decisions as Grace have high impacts when you struggle to take down a single zombie or inventory remains heavily constrained. Leon? Your inventory is massive. You won’t run out of ammo or quips. You’ll be executing rows of zombies in excellent fashion, weaving around the environment with a weighted and grizzled Leon. Like a rusty, but reliable axe that can still split a log on its first swing.  When the game is trading perspectives between characters, it’s firing on all cylinders. Tension waxes and when it peaks, you switch to Leon, waning it down with your trusty handgun, shotgun, and absurd melee attacks. When you trade back to Grace, you feel the anxiety creep back in. You must navigate a care centre reminiscent of classic environments, like the Baker Mansion of RE7. Its got run backs. Its got puzzles. Its got jump scares that are tweaked just enough to still catch you by surprise. In fact, Requiem constantly subverts your expectations. Thought you’d get nearly to the end of the game to find the magnum revolver? Nope, you get it from the start and there’s PLENTY of ammo this time. It’s got cheesy lines. Just the right amount in fact. Mix this all together with excellent lore (files) and this first act and environment boils up to be one of the best, if not THE best segments to date in the series.  And then it stops.   When you reach the second act, your focus shifts to Leon. While there are narrative reasons for it, the game feels at its lowest. It’s as if they were bound to the remnants of the rumoured, original version of the game (open world). The plot grinds to a halt. The quest turns to fetch. You stop swapping with Grace. The puzzles (if any) are derivative. The waxing and waning of tension and release disappears. It simply clashes with the flow that beginning crafted so perfectly.  The good news is that the game DOES return to form, with some additional areas to pick up the pace in the back end of this act. They circle on Leon’s past, and while it’s nice to learn a bit more about Leon’s motivations, its borderline a bit too much. Like a second post credit cutscene from a Marvel movie. If you’re a first timer, or relatively new to the series, I don’t believe there is much for you here either than possibly motivation to go back and play previous entries in Leon’s arc.  The third and final act returns more closely to the beginning. It’s not as tight but the tension and release returns. It concludes with wild and completely over dramatic ending(s) in typical RE fashion. If you’ve played RE before, you know what to expect (or not). If you’re relatively new or this is your first Resident Evil game, don’t sweat it. Try to enjoy it for what it is. Ultimately what marks a great Resident Evil game from a good one is the WANT to go back and replay it immediately.  While Requiem isn’t perfect, and can be down right confusing at times, it plays wonderfully and never forgets the simple fact that it’s a video game.   Don’t over think it. Want to play it all in third person? The option is there. Want to speed run it and just engage with the story on casual mode? Sure. Want to suffer on Insanity mode in first person mode because you’re a masochistic, horror fanatic? I wouldn’t recommend it but why not. It doesn’t matter because that’s a Resident Evil game. No one cares and nor should you.  12 hour completion time. 22 hours Steam time. One month reflecting on Resident Evil Requiem since launch. There are a lot of feelings. Is it the best game in the series? No, I don’t think so. But it’s a damn good time.  Buy it. Play it. Beat it. Play it again. Beat it again. And maybe do that all over again, one more time, but with the infinite rocket launcher spreading meat, blood, and gibs across the halls.  Highly recommend!

And so, my journey through Resident Evil ends (or at least, 2RM, 3RM, 4RM, 7, 8, and 9).   Requiem was my favorite. 9.5/10. Not much here that I didn't love. The setting, the story, the characters, the action-gameplay and the stealth-gameplay were all top-notch.   In particular, I was very impressed with how they handled Grace. Both the writing team and the voice actress did a great job of making you like her almost immediately. Same with Leon, too - he's just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥' cool!   It feels like a "best of" across the franchise, but the story does some really interesting subversions to what you [i]think[/i] is going to happen. Some examples:   [spoiler] At the beginning, Grace's mom tells her, "hey, I can't explain right now because this ♥♥♥♥'s complicated" (I'm paraphrasing, obviously). Turns out - it actually kind of IS complicated. How would someone explain that in 15 seconds while getting chased by a murderer? Compare that to RE8, where Chris tells Ethan, "hey, I know I just shot your wife, but you wouldn't get it so come quietly." Much better execution here. [/spoiler]   [spoiler] Same with the ultimate Elpis twist. Leon's gameplay is telling you DESTROY IT!, but if you really listen to the Spencer/Ashcroft interview, he spells it out really clearly: Elpis is the requiem for the millions of people affected by Spencer's actions, and Grace is the requiem for himself. It's hope. [/spoiler]   I just thought it was really well done. I'm glad I stuck with RE2 after bouncing off it so many times. It was worth it!

[h3]So, what to say about RE:Requiem...[/h3]  Well, frankly in my opinion, the way the story has been written and how the game has been set - it should have been a CG Movie like RE: Death Island, Degeneration etc. But, Capcom made it a game and here we are.  IF you're here because you're expecting sections of the game to play like RE4:Remake - it doesn't. IF you're here because you're expecting sections of the game to play like RE7 or RE8 - it doesn't. (This is based on one playthrough with the standard FPS/3rd Person settings, which you can change if desired.)  The graphics are very good looking, the meshing is great and relatively PC intensive, I'm playing on a Ryzen 7 and 5070 12gb VRAM with 32gb RAM, and it runs quite well - until you run into a specific section and you get frame rate stuttering down to 10-20 frames per second, something in that area is absolutely not optimized. (Turning down mesh options and a few others will get it back to 120fps.) Outside of that section, I had very few stutters or graphics problems. One thing I have to make a mention of, there are reports of when using the Requiem revolver while in Grace sections, on specific OLED monitors your monitor will turn off, restart or go into a power saving mode - be aware of this. (At the time of writing I do not know if there's a solve or patch that fixes this.)  Gameplay wise, it's not that bad, it's not good either - like I mentioned, it will not play like RE4 Remake or RE7 or 8 - it just won't, one thing that I noticed a bit (More so with Leon than Grace) is this, enemies feels like bullet sponges - even with fully upgraded power weapons, that said I never felt like I was low on ammunition either, so with some clever gameplay and weapon choices you should be fine - it just won't feel as fast-paced in the Leon sections as it does with RE4:R.  The Grace sections feels pretty decent, they do feel more like RE7 than 8 to my opinion, the FOV also feels a bit constrained, and there's no native FOV slider and I haven't checked if there are any mods or fixes for this. The enemies doesn't feel as bullet spongy as they do with the Leon sections - you won't run low on ammo, mainly because the game incentivizes you to not shoot everything and instead sneak by. Which I actually kinda like, for me it felt different and fresh - you still have the option though.  Replayability, I don't have much to comment here, there's weapons, items, infinite ammo the entire library of models and stuff you can unlock with CP, and it will take some time getting through all the challenges. So there's that to look for.  [h3]Story[/h3] It's weird -- it really is... There's so much to unpack with this, it feels like it was meant to be a CG movie like I started out saying here in my review, and I stand by that. So many things aren't explained, things happen that have no meaning or impact on the story, and it's a jumble - it's nice to see the Leon "saga" get a supposed ending. (Barring any DLC, which I'm sure will happen.) It's all over the place, the ending just sort of finishes off without answering certain things, and well - that is highly likely a set up for coming DLC. One of the antagonist characters is not explained at all, who is he, why is he here, he isn't in any of the CG movies, he's just there...  [h3]Anyway, I'll finish off.[/h3] If you're a massive fan of the Resident Evil series, particularly RE4/RE4:R, and RE7 and 8 - you probably really want to play this game. Just don't buy the deluxe edition unless it's something you really want, or is on sale - there's no reason to get the deluxe pack at all.  Is it worth the price of admission, eh - I'm a frugal person, so I'll say no, if you have the patience to wait on sale, get it on sale. If you have to get it now and you're willing to take a few changes in how it feels compared to what you're used to - get the game, just don't expect to get what you've been getting since the 2/3/4 remakes or 7 and 8. It's close enough to say "same same, but slightly different."  Whatever you choose, thanks for reading. Have a good'un.

This may actually be the best resident evil to date, and very much IS the best of the modern, non remake, games.   Game design wise it takes the best mechanics and design philosophy from the series goats like village's horror and atmosphere and combines it with resident evil 4/5s action. Each with their own respective segments so they dont impede on each other.   My recommendation for your first playthrough is pick either of the standard difficulty settings depending on the level of challenge you're comfortable with as these 2 modes are truly the intended way to play your first run, while the horror is still fresh. On my first playthrough of this game, I was having a pretty solid time. I thoroughly enjoyed the more explorable areas, felt a bit tense at some of the Grace sections, and had a blast with Leon's action sections. The story kind of played in the background for me because at first glance it wasn't anything all that special. Very standard issue "evil people doing shady experiment stuff." I completed the game, looked at all the fun-sounding things I could unlock for New Game+, and headed right back in to start completing challenges. That's when the recency bias fell of rapidly and hard.  I started a Casual (Easy) difficulty run to complete the harder challenges (gather no "crafting material" as Grace, use no healing items), so surviving became an afterthought and I could take in the areas, environments, enemy design, story, and characters better. Having now completed all achievements, I can safely say I don't think I ever want to return to this game.  Positives: - The gunplay feels very good and upgrades feel significant, powerful, and are visually shown in model changes when you gain access to them (charms with added effects feel far more hit or miss). - The Care Center for Grace and Leon's explorable area I found quite fun to path through, although I wish they were longer sections. - Graphically the game is gorgeous. Absolutely no complaints from a visual standpoint.  Negatives: - Characters elicited either indifference or annoyance, which is particularly sad when the annoyance comes from one of the protagonists. Grace is supposedly an FBI agent, but seems to be in a perpetual state of panic no matter the situation or who she's with. Leon is cool and quippy, but frequently sits around doing nothing as people die because "it's cutscene time." The villains are....there, one of whom is introduced late in the game just to have nothing done with him. - The story is completely nonsensical. When the villain's whole plan hinges on one specific person being alive, they probably shouldn't be doing everything in their power to either kill him/her or leave him/her in extremely dangerous situations that will get him/her killed. The story also not only retcons major past events in the series from my cursory knowledge of it, but also retcons itself in really silly ways at points. - Enemy variety seems diverse at first, but you rapidly realize that most enemies are just reskins, or when new enemies are introduced, they get vastly underused or weirdly utilized. Many enemy/boss types feel like either potentially nostalgia-bait or "why is this thing here, in this setting?" - Swapping between Grace and Leon (and subsequently horror and action) sounded cool in concept, but was tonally jarring in the end, especially when many, many sections end up being extremely short, thinly-veiled hallways or "loop the monster once or twice" encounters with seemingly roaming creatures that turn out to be heavily scripted instead. - There aren't really puzzles in this game, which took me far too long to realize. Pretty much every "puzzle" turns out to be "you got this item, put it where it obviously goes," or "push buttons based on the thing right behind you on the desk." I can only think of maybe one exception, but even that was "find the thing that directly tells you the solution," no thinking required. - I started dreading most of Grace's sections, especially after Leon. This dread came from Grace's movement being very, very sluggish in comparison to Leon, which I guess makes sense in context, but really doesn't feel great to play. - While being priced at our lovely new standard of $70, a normal playthrough takes about 10-11 hours, with the only current post-game being essentially "Do it again."  Ultimately, the game was a decent enough experience, at least in the gameplay department, when I wasn't thinking too deeply about it the first time through. If not for my completionist nature, I feel like I would have given up early on in the second playthrough, however. Replay value feels very low now, because the more I played through again, the more I just wanted to be done with it.

[b]And here we go again – the ultimate heartbreaker is out there saving someone...[/b]  As the developers recommended, I played the game the intended way: on standard difficulty, first-person for Grace and third-person for Leon.  First of all, credit where it’s due – Capcom has clearly mastered their formula with the RE Engine. The game looks stunning. High-end visuals, ray tracing, lighting, shadows, animations – everything you’d expect from a AAA title. I doubt anyone will have complaints about the visuals. That said, playing in first person almost makes you miss out on some of the excellent character animations – switching perspectives really shows how much effort went into them.  The audio design is easily one of the most impressive I’ve experienced. It shines the most during Grace’s segments, where gameplay heavily relies on sound. The opening sequence and hotel prologue are outstanding, especially with good headphones. The tension is incredibly well-crafted, and throughout the game, sound constantly keeps you on edge – perfectly fitting her playstyle.  [b]Now, Grace’s gameplay[/b]. I’m not a huge fan of pure horror games [i](though I’m fine with horror when there are weapons involved)[/i]. At first, this feels like a textbook horror experience – genuinely tense and uncomfortable in a good way. You often find yourself in stressful situations where you have to react quickly and inevitably make mistakes, which somehow adds to the experience.  I’m usually not a fan of backtracking, but here it’s handled fairly well. Locations evolve, new events occur, and it never feels completely static – which is also a staple of the series.  It’s been a while since a game made me react this strongly to horror elements. Sound design, visual effects, and scripted events all work together to create a genuinely scary atmosphere. Until you learn the layout and enemy behavior, you’ll spend a lot of time hiding and playing cautiously. Limited saves also push you into a more careful, old-school survival approach.  Enemies deserve praise too – just when you think you’ve figured them out, they can still surprise you. Grace’s sections are full of tense, memorable moments.  However, the gameplay starts to drag in the second half. Objectives become repetitive – fuses, switches, generators, keys [i](always in sets of three)[/i], and a persistent unkillable enemy chasing you around. It gets tiring. On standard difficulty, I had to play very cautiously to avoid losing progress.  Eventually, you get used to the horror. Which raises a question – what’s the point of replaying it when all the scripted scares are already known?  [b]Now, Leon[/b]. His gameplay initially felt a bit disappointing – especially since I had recently played Resident Evil 4. It feels very familiar, almost unchanged. It was even a bit frustrating that I had already cleared an area, leaving Leon with little to do there.  The second half improves things with semi-open areas and more freedom. After Grace, this feels like a breath of fresh air. Still, the objectives remain repetitive – again with fuses and batteries.  Fan service is handled well – returning to Raccoon City and the police station was a highlight. I’m not even a hardcore fan, but that segment worked really well thanks to nostalgia.  Progression and upgrades in the second half feel familiar and satisfying – a welcome addition.  That said, after playing Leon, Grace’s sections start to feel overly stretched. Just as you get used to one character, the game switches you to another. The pacing feels uneven, though perhaps that contrast is intentional.  One thing I really appreciated is the map design – markers for locked doors are a blessing. No need to take notes manually [i](I never thought that this would end up being a plus for me)[/i]  Cons:  – The first-person FOV is terrible. It genuinely caused discomfort. I couldn’t figure out what was wrong for hours. There’s no setting to fix it, so I had to install a mod, which breaks immersion. This wasn’t an issue in Resident Evil 7 or Village.  – Boss fights are underwhelming. There are few of them, and they mostly boil down to dealing damage without much variation.  – Puzzles are too simple, even for me. The storytelling is also very on-the-nose – camera angles and hints often spoil upcoming events.  – The story... well, if you don’t think too hard about it, it’s fine.  - Despite its strengths, the price feels a bit steep. This is a very safe continuation of Resident Evil, combining two familiar gameplay styles without introducing anything [i]new[/i].  - The horror works best the first time – after that, it’s just mechanics. Leon’s gameplay is solid but nothing we haven’t seen before.  Final thoughts:  I got the game as a gift, but I wouldn’t be fully convinced at full price. At a 50% discount, though – absolutely worth it.  As I said, I'm not a fan, but I enjoy every new game in this series. And thankfully, the games in this series still haven't disappointed players yet.

How do we make a game for both newcomers and hardcore fans? For decades, the answer has been: we can't really. Hardcore fans tend to hate change, while onboarding newcomers usually come at the cost of adding Quality of Life features every single other game has these days to make it more welcoming, always at the risk of diluting what made the original one unique by making it like everything else.  Capcom has solved this though and the answer is: Just game two games lmao  Resident Evil Requiem isn't really one game, it's two games, the first half is one thing with flashes of another things, the second half is almost entirely the other thing, with flashes to the first thing and it is insane to go through the same enviroments, facing the same enemies as two different protagonists: Grace, who has to hide from everything and line up shots because she has almost no ammo the whole time, and Leon, who just chainsaws and shotguns everything that comes across him. It's insane.  But what's truly important to me is that in the Grace segments we get the return of the crimson heads from REmake 1, which is the possibility that every zombie that you don't headshot can come back insanely faster and stronger when you backtrack through an area, we got ink ribbons, limiting your number of saves, hell, the examine function, barely used in most survival horror games, is used a ridiculous number of times here, almost like a vengeance for decades of being mostly ignored. This is peak survival horror, the developers added maximum friction while respecting the inteligence of the average player more than 90% of AAA studios these days.  And the Leon segment is not far behind, putting you through enemy filled arena after enemy filled arena, through dark corridor ambush after dark corridor ambush, the parrying knife from REmake 4 returns, this time as a parrying hatchet allowing to parry almost anything thrown your way, I personally find the decision to shove hundreds of zombies in your way, but making them weaker compared to the REmake games to be a hit straight in the bullseye, this is very personal, but I would rather fight a hundred weak enemies than a dozen bullet sponges, the felling of watching them fall like a sack of potatoes when you nail a headshot is one of the most satisfying feeling in the worlds.  I don't know how to finish this review so I guess I will state that I did not 100% any of the Resident Evil games on Steam, except for Requiem. Take this a sign of extreme quality, this is not a game you want to miss. Though it's focus on returning to the past and nostalgia might make it for a poor first entry into the franchise. Start from REmake and then work your way here, either through the originals or the remakes, though I should warn you those are very different past the first remake and you might want to play both paths at the same time for best results, they are all available on Steam as of recently, so go wild.

I wish I could give a mixed review, but given the overwhelmingly positive rating the game already has, I think it should balance out.  Resident Evil: Requiem is a bipolar experience that varies greatly in quality in both objective and subjective ways. How much you will enjoy this game depends heavily on why you play RE titles, and how much nostalgia affects you.  Without any spoilers, the game is split into two halves, both for gameplay and story. Playing as Grace during the first half of the game is some of the best Resident Evil I have ever experienced, easily up there with the original trilogy and Remake 2. The mansion-esque level combined with the most interesting form of zombie the series has presented, it's top shelf gaming. Leon appears infrequently, counter-balancing the intense and oppressive survival horror with bursts of all-out action similar to Remake 4, allowing you to bend the tension over backwards and show it who's boss for a brief stretch.  Meanwhile, the story keeps a sparse, but intriguing presence, giving you just enough breadcrumbs to keep interests high and theories forming. It's clear that Grace is the protagonist, with Leon being a supporting character, and that works perfectly for the story being presented. Unfortunately, the game cannot keep this pace.  While RE titles are no stranger to losing steam part-way through, this is one of the sharpest drops in quality I have seen in the series, nearly topping RE7's tanker level. Instead of playing as Grace with bursts of Leon, you now have a six hour Leon segment in gray and brown post-apocalyptic concrete jungles filled with the same three enemy types, and while Leon's gameplay is quite enjoyable, even the best will wear thin without variety. This is also where the story takes a nosedive.  I can't really spoil this section of the game, since nothing of consequence even happens. What I can say is that they went all in on nostalgia, and while it makes some sense given the setting, certain parts are leaps and bounds above logic, jumping straight into absurdity with the hopes of blind nostalgia holding your interest.  [If you want to go in completely blind, skip this paragraph.] It's hard to put into words how poor the story is overall, let alone in the last half, but just know that none of the mystery actually matters, it retcons multiple characters (bordering on character assassination), does a poor job of utilizing Grace and Leon, has possibly one of the worst villains in the series, and never answers half the questions it brings up. I don't wanna say this the worst RE story, but it definitely feels the most slap-dashed of recent titles.  Despite a poor story, I can forgive a lot if the replays and gameplay are enjoyable. Unfortunately, RE9 has some of the worst replayability, nearly topping Remake 3. You have the usual suspects with infinite ammo, infinite durability for melee weapons, and some special weapons, but upgrades don't carry over from Leon, and the weapons are really just pre-upgraded variations that you'll use against the same gray enemies. Meanwhile, Grace only gets one special gun that isn't particularly good or interesting. To be frank, this is utter ♥♥♥♥. On top of this, the idea of replaying this game makes me shudder with the sheer quantity and duration of scripted story sections that act as cutscenes with death animations. No, they didn't learn their lesson from RE7 or RE8 and how much people complained about their protracted openings.  Overall, I can't say I didn't enjoy my time with RE9, but there were a handful of points in the latter half where I almost quit, and replaying it for completion became a chore rather than a joy. I can tentatively recommend this game to RE fans, but anyone looking for a quality story, strong replayability, or a solid entry point for the rest of the series, look elsewhere.
