[h1] A good game ultimately, a bottom 3 installment effectively. [/h1]  [b]It feels like an exclusive sequel to RE2R, but decided to leave out 90% of every single detail not named [spoiler]Sherry[/spoiler] or Leon.[/b]  RE9: Requiem is an excellent game, yet an EXTREMELY LACKING numbered Resident Evil installment. While I do recommend this game to all fans new and old, the more older fans play it, the more they should take notice to issues revolving around this game's approach to memes, and single-dimensional writing. There is A LOT MISSING from this game. Even the writing makes no sense from Leon's perspective for so much of what's missing.  If you're new to Resident Evil, this isn't the best place to start, but it's actually a good one to get you to explore earlier titles afterwards. It's very fun, modern and accessible to new players, even if you're scared of everything.   Resident Evil 9: Requiem thrives entirely on fan-service. It has a very misunderstood attention to detail of what made RE2 so great to begin with. It's like a delicious steak, the sinfully unctuous marbling, and they just hand you a tray of rendered fat in a pool of oil and nothing of substance to bite into. It's an unbalanced mess that thinks it's giving you what makes meat a high-grade, with no understanding what what the eater wants or has always enjoyed of it.  There's so much deliberate design to the first and third person schemes that enhance gameplay from either perspective(third-person for Grace you can run much faster during certain sequences, but you trip, and from Leon's end, first person is extremely smooth transitions when you go for kicks, and executions). There's clear love and care for hyper-specific animations and interactions, and yet all this attention to detail just to neglect the core basic concepts of old school RE. That it just feels like bells, whistles and jingling keys, which is an insane statement to say after they made RE2R in 2019.  Grace's section is excellent for the first locale, the rest throughout the game feel SO MUCH WORSE. The first location will have you looping around for a couple hours to put a key here, a lockpick there, an enemy spawns on your backtrack. It's very true to the RE formula of running back and forth however, every section after the first location is completely 100% linear...? Grace also gets... no gun variety whatsoever??? How in the world did we go from RE7's John "Everyman" Ethan with a full loadout to Grace with 1 pistol the entire game.  Leon is extremely overpowered(fun) and armed to his teeth. He makes me goo-goo gaga at just how rigid and seasoned he's become but they've eased into his one-liners and memes so much to the point I'm completely prepared for Capcom to make Chris just say "Leon ♥♥♥♥ my sister and continue the bloodline".   Here's one of my personal problems with Leon for RE9. We have no "fun" guns, no dart launcher, no bolt-thrower, no Chicago typewriter, no PRL-412, no striker, no minigun or sparkshot, no quad-missile, no flamethrower, no grenade launcher. If Resident Evil Requiem is anything like what it’s teasing to be, we’re in for another round of “why did I agree to go into this place?” energy—and honestly, that’s exactly what I want from this series.  Even from what we’ve seen so far, it feels like Capcom is leaning back into that slow-burn dread the franchise is famous for, where every hallway feels like a bad decision and every sound makes you reconsider your entire build. You know the vibe: low supplies, high anxiety, and the constant suspicion that something is absolutely about to sprint at you from off-screen.  What I’m hoping for is that classic Resident Evil balance—tense exploration, smart puzzles, and combat that makes every bullet feel like it costs you emotionally. And if they keep leaning into modern presentation like RE7 and RE8 did, it could be another “turn off the lights and regret everything” masterpiece.  Also, let’s be real: every Resident Evil game needs at least one moment where the protagonist says something like:  * “This can’t be happening…” * “Okay, nope. Absolutely not.” * or the classic internal monologue of *why am I still here?*  If Requiem delivers that mix of dread, chaos, and occasional absurdity the series is known for, it’s going to hit hard.  Only downside? I’m already mentally preparing to pause the game just to stare at a door for 30 seconds before opening it.  Overall: cautiously hyped/10. If it sticks the landing, it could be another unforgettable entry in the series of beautiful disasters that is Resident Evil.

Excellent addition to the RE series.  It's a tricky knife edge they walked merging Leon's action packed gameplay with Grace's slower, more traditional RE style but the devs managed it.  Capcom did something similar to what Valve did with Half-life in using action and puzzle sections to control the game's pacing and avoid fatigue from either style of play. With that said, it's not as perfected as Half-Life.  There are moments in both Grace and Leon's segments where they pacing feels off.  Some of Grace's parts can drag on a bit too long and a few of Leon's earlier segments can feel too quick. It has lots of wonderful callbacks to the original RE games that are done well and don't feel like pandering.  Capcom is still using the adaptive difficulty in this one which can cause some mild confusion or frustration when it comes to getting a feel for how much damage you are doing and how much you can take.  However, it does feel like it has been adjusted a little and the difficulty creep for skilled players is not as sudden as it was in RE2R. The story is pretty good for a Resident Evil game and Capcom has continued their trend of more naturalistic dialogue that started in RE2R.  It makes the story feel a little more grounded and mature.  Story tension is well done, feels like writer took a page out of Jurassic Park's book on how to create and hold tension.  What I mean by that is a tense scene will kick off and the stakes will start to be raised incrementally until it is honed to a fine point before finally releasing it.  This was done very well throughout the game and you can tell a lot of attention was put on this to make it perfect. Only wrinkle I have with the story is a small one, the villains identity crisis they seem to be having.  Gideon at first feels like the main villain but acts more like a henchman and spends a lot of the story in this henchman role until way late into the story.  Zeno presents as the main villain through most of the story but is actually fulfilling the henchman role.  It is a little confusing the first time through and might leave people wondering what the whole point of even having Zeno around was.  If you look deeper and analyze the story a little this role confusion these two have starts to make more sense but RE games have never been good at being "deep" so there is no precedence for having characters with much depth so there is no impetus for the player to see them as anything else than their surface level presentation.  Overall it was a genuinely fun game and I am looking forward to the DLC when it releases.

Overall it left a rather unpleasant aftertaste. If you feel like you won’t be able to resist buying it because of the marketing hype, I’d say wait for a sale—or go back to older RE titles depending on what this game offers that appeals to you (RE2R or RE7 for Grace-style gameplay, RE4R or even RE6 for Leon).  Despite my disappointment, I don’t want to undersell the game entirely—some phases of Grace’s clinic and cell block sections, the strong opening, and the way past gameplay experience and craftsmanship have been partially recreated with visible effort deserve some credit. Yet evaluating with the rest, this game absolutely does not deserve the level of praise and attention it’s getting, and I think it represents a step backward for the series.  I don’t even know where to begin. Let’s start with the dual-character structure and the overall presentation. Some spoilers ahead.  Grace’s sections start with strong momentum but gradually lose it. It devolves into a loop of collecting blood from the environment and crafting equipment to kill enemies, while also hiding from stalkers and waiting them out. This creates a contradiction with how Grace is portrayed in the story. If you’re even a moderately skilled player, Grace turns into a female Rambo—popping stabilizers like performance enhancers, blowing everything up with infected blood syringes, and mowing down nearly everything except unkillable stalkers. Yet in cutscenes and scripted moments, her voice keeps trembling.  Grace, you just calmly hunted and killed an entire clinic full of people under the logic of survival—why are you still shaking or tripping while running? And why are you still so obsessively fixated on Emily when her condition is obvious? What about everyone else in the clinic?   Sure, Emily is a child and you have a trauma bond—but at some point, like Leon shooting down abominations, you should be able to “let it go.” As it stands, Grace comes off as weak, irrational, overly emotional, and reactive in every situation. It makes you question how she can be so cold-blooded and efficient under player control while being so inconsistent narratively.  This also creates pacing issues with Leon’s segments early on. When you switch to Leon, there’s barely anything left besides loot that only he can access. He deals with a few extra enemies at the beginning or end of his segment, then you’re thrown back into 2–3 hours of dragging gameplay with Grace. But as I said, this isn’t really survival anymore—you’re not prey, you’re the predator. Grace clearly has a Lara Croft buried inside her, but the game never reflects that in her character development or dialogue. It’s a strange disconnect.  You can’t really say you “play as Leon” until the story shifts to Raccoon City. Much like Ada in Separate Ways, Leon gets promoted from side character to main character there, and the second half of the game is largely his. Unfortunately, his sections feel very generic. Aside from a few cinematic moments—like navigating a collapsed skyscraper or escaping a rooftop filled with mortar-firing zombies—the Raccoon City quarantine gate and RPD areas feel sterile and industrial, very much like RE3R. They’re repetitive, linear, and frankly empty. It feels like leftover assets from an early multiplayer/open-world development phase—especially the final Umbrella Ark Laboratory, which looks like reused RE3R lab content.  With Leon, you can upgrade gear via a military-style electronic supply box based on kills and wristbands collected. But compared to the Merchant in RE4R or the Duke in Village, the system is extremely limited and soulless. The UI isn’t user-friendly either—it feels like something ripped from a futuristic online FPS, but stripped of depth.  As for Leon’s combat: while the parry system somewhat resembles RE4R, the overall feel sits awkwardly between RE6 and RE4R. Weapons don’t evolve meaningfully over time. His handgun feels slow and weak—even after upgrades, it only becomes mediocre. Other weapons suffer the same issue: they fire sluggishly, almost like they’re jamming.  In short, aside from bolt-action sniper rifles, none of Leon’s weapons feel as powerful, weighty, or responsive as in RE4R. They’re closer to RE6—and worse, enemies are spongey and unresponsive, again like RE6. They rarely get stunned, making Leon’s added melee finishers and combat moves mostly pointless.   Remember that flashy clinic showcase where Leon pulls off all those cool moves? That’s pure marketing illusion. That’s basically the only segment where those mechanics are used effectively—and there are no additional animations beyond what was shown there.  Another issue: in RE4R, resources were always scarce. Here, unless you’re a terrible shot, resources pile up. This kills tension. I constantly had +10 shotgun or sniper ammo, and even when those ran out, I still had +200 SMG rounds.  As a result, every boss fight became trivial: parry, then spam shotgun or SMG for 2 minutes. Tyrant/Mr. X, Commander, Gideon—they’re all extremely underwhelming.  The writing and story are shockingly bad—even by RE standards. It contradicts the established universe and undermines it with unnecessary retcons. The character roster is barren, which is surprising for a series known for memorable personalities. Expecting villains like Heisenberg or Dimitrescu? Forget it. Strong female characters like Ada, Jill, Claire, or Sheva? Forget that too. Grace doesn’t count—she’s bland and poorly written.  The voice actress does a good job, but the character itself is inconsistent and illogical, as explained earlier.  The retcon of Spencer—portrayed as having a conscience and sabotaging his own legacy—is completely out of character. It’s like claiming Wesker was secretly a good person. The newly introduced elements—Raccoon City Syndrome and Elpis—are equally damaging. If viral bioweapons are neutralized, what even remains of the RE universe?  The writing is so careless that it contradicts itself within the same game. At one point, Sherry claims the Pentagon never ordered the destruction of Raccoon City—but later, Grace’s FBI report repeatedly states that the U.S. government did it under pressure from bioweapon lobbies. Which is it?  Even worse, the government denying past wrongdoing makes no sense when the FBI—under that same government—has documented it. And this was already established lore: the city was destroyed to cover up Umbrella’s actions. Replacing T- or G-Virus with Elpis doesn’t add anything new—it just creates inconsistencies. If Elpis existed, Ada in RE2R would’ve been after that instead.  These retcons don’t expand the lore—they clash with it. The “new Umbrella facility under Raccoon City” twist is especially lazy.  And with something like Raccoon City Syndrome in play, it’s absurd that only Sherry is treated while others just wait around, and Leon goes on a suicide mission while infected. It’s clearly written to push Leon into the spotlight, reducing others—including Grace—to mere tools for his character.  Maybe I should give it a 6/10. But ultimately, gameplay and design matter most, and despite its flaws, the game stands on the shoulders of past experience.  If this were a movie or book, I’d give it a 3 or 4 out of 10.  Like every RE game, does it still make you feel like you’re playing through a horror zombie film? Yes, it does. But overall, it feels like a sterile, overly commercial product that takes the series backward.  A disappointment for me.  Imo, it doesn’t even come close to RE4R. 😀  If you want action-horror with Leon, play RE4R. If you want survival horror like Grace, play RE1R, RE2R, or RE7. All of those execute their focus better than Requiem.  Buy this one on sale.  At this price, it offers an 10 hour campaign that feels like two RE3R-length runs. Replayability is low, pacing is uneven, content is lacking, and there’s no extra gameplay mode to this date. Meanwhile, RE4R Gold Edition offers two excellent campaigns plus a rich Mercenaries.

I didn’t expect Resident Evil Requiem to feel this… personal.  At first, I thought it was just another entry trying to balance horror and action like the series always does. But the more I played, the more it became clear that this game is doing something a little different. It’s not just about surviving—it’s about ending something.  What really stood out to me is how the game handles its two playable perspectives.  Playing as Grace is honestly stressful in the best way. Her sections lean heavily into slow, creeping horror. You’re constantly low on resources, the spaces feel tight and oppressive, and there’s this lingering sense that something is always nearby. It’s not just jump scares—it’s the kind of tension that builds quietly and doesn’t really go away. I found myself moving slower, checking corners more, and just feeling uneasy the whole time.  Then the game shifts to Leon S. Kennedy—and it’s such a noticeable change, but in a good way. It almost feels like a release of pressure. You’re still dealing with dangerous situations, but now you actually have the experience and tools to fight back. The combat feels solid, and instead of pure fear, it becomes more about control and survival under pressure. It doesn’t turn into full-on action, but it definitely gives you room to breathe.  What impressed me the most is how smooth the transition between the two is. It never feels jarring. The pacing just naturally shifts from Grace’s anxiety-heavy sections to Leon’s more controlled gameplay. That balance keeps the tension going without ever feeling repetitive.  Story-wise, the title “Requiem” really fits. There’s a sense throughout the game that it’s wrapping things up—especially when it comes to Umbrella and everything tied to it. It feels reflective, like the series is looking back at its own history while slowly moving forward. By the end, it genuinely feels like a closing chapter, but also the start of something new.  Overall, I think Resident Evil Requiem does a great job respecting what came before while still pushing things in a new direction. It’s tense, well-paced, and surprisingly thoughtful.  If this really is a send-off for that part of the series, then it’s a pretty strong one.

RE9, to me, feels like a very ambitious entry to the franchise, making so many new cool mechanics and features, all while it still contains the core fundamentals of earlier titles. The story is nice, I would say on par with the better RE games, and the characters are enjoyable. Leon is great as always, but the performance of Grace is easily the best in the game, which adds to her already amazing segments in the story.[spoiler] I do wish she got more spotlight near the latter half of the game.[/spoiler]  I won't say much, but the first section of the game is one of the best RE experiences of all time, it feels so refreshing and dynamic, and it offers a perfect balance of difficulty without being an annoyance. On top of that, switching between Grace's horror segments to Leon's more action-like gameplay is perfectly paced in this part of the game, and there's no better joy than absolutely blazing a room that was horrifying an hour or two ago.  And speaking of it, the combat in the game feels really good. I wouldn't say it's as good as RE4R or RE6, but it holds up on its own. The sounds definitely improve upon it, with the game having maybe the best sound design in RE, as well as any horror game I've played.  The game is perhaps one of the longest in the game (which I think is a good thing), and while it feels pretty linear at times, there are a lot of segments that reward exploration.  My main issue with the game is one very prominent bug that I have seen discussed by many, which is that cutscenes will VERY frequently have audio desync, which ruins the immersion immensely, to the point where I'd have to watch YouTube clips of them every so often. This likely won't be a problem if your PC is relatively new, but if your computer runs on duct tape and vibes like mine, then beware this issue.   With that being said, gameplay performance, on the other hand, was great, I was able to stay at 60fps with very minimal stutters, which is great for me. I hope CAPCOM can continue their hot streak of optimization, and I really hope they fix this audio bug early for any newcomers to the game.

Das ist kein kleiner Satz, weil Resident Evil schon über Jahrzehnte zu den stärksten Namen im Horror-Genre gehört. Aber Requiem hat bei mir genau das geschafft, was nur ganz wenige Spiele schaffen: Es hat mich nicht nur unterhalten, sondern komplett gepackt, überrascht, mitgerissen und teilweise regelrecht emotional erwischt. Für mich ist das hier nicht einfach nur ein starkes Resident Evil. Das ist aktuell mein persönliches Game of the Year.  Gameplay und Combat: 10/10 ohne Diskussion  Das Erste, was mich komplett abgeholt hat, war das Gameplay. Resident Evil 9 fühlt sich nicht einfach nur gut an – es fühlt sich so an, als hätte Capcom ganz genau verstanden, was dieses Franchise spielerisch so stark macht, und dann alles auf ein neues Level gehoben. Der Spielfluss ist brutal stark, das Pacing sitzt, die Steuerung fühlt sich direkt an und das gesamte Spiel erzeugt permanent dieses Gefühl aus Spannung, Druck und Kontrolle. Auch der Combat ist für mich eine glatte 10/10. Jeder Kampf hat Wucht, jeder Treffer fühlt sich passend an und man hat nie das Gefühl, dass das Spiel sich irgendwie träge oder unsauber spielt. Es ist genau diese Mischung aus Überlebenskampf, Druck und Präzision, die Resident Evil schon immer gebraucht hat – nur hier wirkt alles noch sauberer, stärker und intensiver. Es ist nicht einfach nur “gut gemacht”, sondern so gut, dass ich wirklich sagen würde: So stark hat sich Resident Evil für mich noch nie gespielt.  Atmosphäre: So viel Angst hatte ich noch nie  Und jetzt zum vielleicht wichtigsten Punkt: die Atmosphäre. Ich habe wirklich schon viele Horror-Spiele gespielt, auch viele harte Sachen – aber ich hatte noch nie so viel Angst in einem Horror-Spiel wie hier. Und das meine ich genau so. Resident Evil 9 schafft es, dich konstant unter Spannung zu halten. Nicht nur mit billigen Schockmomenten, sondern mit echter, unangenehmer, schwerer Horror-Atmosphäre. Das Spiel baut Druck auf, ohne dass es ständig laut werden muss. Es erzeugt dieses Gefühl, dass jederzeit etwas passieren könnte. Räume wirken bedrohlich, Wege wirken unsicher, jede Ecke kann falsch sein. Genau das ist für mich großer Horror: nicht nur erschrecken, sondern dieses ständige Unwohlsein, diese Nervosität, dieses “Ich will weiter, aber ich hab eigentlich keinen Bock, da jetzt reinzugehen”. Und Resident Evil 9 macht das auf absolutem Top-Niveau.  Story: Besser hätte es nicht sein können  Ich übertreibe hier nicht, wenn ich sage: Die Story hätte für mich nicht besser sein können. Gerade bei Resident Evil ist das immer so ein Punkt, wo die Reihe manchmal zwischen Camp, Kult und echter emotionaler Wirkung schwankt. Aber Requiem hat mich hier voll erwischt. Die Geschichte funktioniert nicht nur als Rahmen für Horror und Action, sondern trägt das Spiel wirklich mit. Sie fühlt sich wichtig an. Sie fühlt sich groß an. Und vor allem fühlt sie sich so an, als würde sie genau das liefern, was man sich von einem Titel dieser Größe wünscht. Für mich war das kein Fall von “Gameplay stark, Story halt da”. Nein – hier war auch die Story auf Top-Niveau. Das macht das ganze Erlebnis am Ende noch stärker, weil es eben nicht nur spielerisch knallt, sondern auch emotional hängen bleibt.  Hunk-Bossfight: 11/10  Ein riesiges Highlight für mich war ganz klar der Hunk-Bossfight. Und ehrlich: 11/10. Anders kann ich’s nicht sagen. Das war einer von diesen Momenten, wo du als Spieler einfach nur da sitzt und dir denkst: Ja man, genau dafür zocke ich sowas. Der Kampf hatte Präsenz, Druck, Stil und genau diese besondere Energie, die einen Bossfight von “gut” zu “legendär” macht. Solche Momente bleiben hängen. Nicht nur, weil sie spielerisch stark sind, sondern weil sie sich groß anfühlen. Besonders. Bedeutend. Genau so ein Fight war das für mich.  Leon im RPD: Einer dieser Gaming-Momente  Und dann kam dieser Moment, der mich komplett gebrochen hat: Als Leon das RPD betreten hat, musste ich wirklich weinen, weil es so schön war. Mehr muss man eigentlich fast gar nicht sagen. Das ist genau die Art von Szene, die zeigt, wie stark ein Spiel sein kann, wenn es Gameplay, Atmosphäre, Fanservice, Emotionen und Inszenierung perfekt zusammendenkt. Dieser Moment war nicht einfach nur “cool” oder “nostalgisch”, sondern wirklich emotional. Er hatte Gewicht. Er hatte Seele. Und genau solche Szenen machen aus einem sehr guten Spiel ein unvergessliches Spiel.  Technik und Performance: Besser als gedacht  Technisch war ich positiv überrascht. Die Performance war besser, als ich erwartet hatte, und gerade bei so einem Spiel ist das extrem wichtig. Horror lebt von Timing, Stimmung und Immersion – und wenn die Technik ständig nervt, reißt dich das sofort raus. Aber hier hatte ich deutlich mehr Vertrauen ins Gesamtpaket, als ich anfangs gedacht hätte. Dass so ein atmosphärisch dichtes Spiel dann auch technisch ordentlich läuft, hebt das Erlebnis nochmal deutlich an. Es sorgt einfach dafür, dass man sich komplett auf das konzentrieren kann, was wirklich zählt: die Welt, die Spannung, die Kämpfe und die Story.  Was war das Beste am Spiel? Ganz einfach: alles  Normalerweise kann man bei einem Spiel sagen: Das war der stärkste Part, das war eher schwächer, da gab’s kleinere Hänger. Bei Resident Evil 9 ist mein ehrlicher Eindruck aber: Das Geilste am Spiel war für mich das gesamte Spiel. Das klingt erstmal übertrieben, aber genau so hat es sich angefühlt. Es gab nicht diesen einen Aspekt, der alles getragen hat. Es war das Gesamtpaket. Das Zusammenspiel aus Gameplay, Combat, Horror, Story, Bosskämpfen, Fanservice, Emotionen und Atmosphäre war für mich einfach so stark, dass ich am Ende nicht sagen will: “Ja, das und das war besonders gut.” Ich will eher sagen: Das ganze Ding war eine Wucht.  Fazit  Resident Evil 9: Requiem ist für mich nicht nur ein fantastisches Horror-Spiel, sondern der beste Teil der Reihe. Und das sage ich als jemand, der fast alle RE-Spiele gezockt hat. Dieses Spiel hat mich spielerisch komplett überzeugt, atmosphärisch zerstört, emotional erwischt und mit einzelnen Momenten beschenkt, die ich so schnell sicher nicht vergessen werde

I enjoyed the game a lot. The graphics are amazing, the sound is great, the English voice acting is top, and the character, monster, and environment design are peak.  I’ve known the RE genre for a while, but this is the first game I played myself. I usually have motion sickness when playing games, but I was super happy that I was not forced to play in first-person perspective. That helped a lot, and overall I had no problems here with that, so great job!  As I said before, the graphics are outstanding, and you don’t need a 5k gaming PC to run this game (of course not on the highest settings if you have a potato PC, but the game still looks awesome even on low settings). The models are really well made, with great textures and rigging, and didn’t give me any uncanny vibes (besides some enemies, but this is probably on purpose, it is a horror game, lmao).  I played the game on normal/easy because I just wanted to enjoy the game and have fun with exploration and lore. I never felt negatively stressed by the game. It had a lot of action with Leon and some scary parts with Grace. The split between these two was a really good gameplay decision, so everybody gets a piece of the cake. But I am a bit sad that Leon’s parts didn’t get as much playtime. At the end, yes, but at the beginning I wish I could fight way more, because it was super fun to kick, shoot, and fight through stuff. The gameplay was so dynamic, it was so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ entertaining!  I liked most of the puzzles. They were pretty understandable, and even though the game is not open world, it was still a lot of fun to explore every corner. So many details in the environment, so many puzzles. But to be honest, some of them gave me RE7 vibes, where they didn’t make much sense. For example, why do I need three cubes with symbols in a hospital to open a door? Maybe I could find three special keycards from each doctor or something, that would fit the modern setting better. Also, I need to give props to the person who designed Victor’s room. The DNA asset mechanism was really great, a small detail, but really well made. I liked it a lot.  The gore in the game is also really good, parts are falling off, monsters are melting, and you can see all the details. Technically and artistically, really fabulous.  Also, the skins are worth it, they look really pretty!  I also love the fact that the concept art is kind of free, you only need to pay with in-game currency that you get from playing. Sadly not common these days anymore, pretty often behind paywalls. I’m happy that it is free here. A lot of free art I can look at, I love seeing the concept art.  This game feels like a good mix of action and horror, kind of like the best parts of RE2 Remake, RE4 Remake, and RE7.  Me recommend!

It is highly story-driven and engaging, with excellent gameplay and cutscenes. It also learns well from the series’ past, combining the best of the RE2-4 golden era with the “back to the origins” approach of RE7-8.  My only criticism is that it does not come close to RE4, and I think the main reason is its linearity. In RE4, you explore a fairly large rural region of Spain, which makes the experience feel much more immersive. By contrast, RE9 feels more like a sequence of isolated areas.  That said, hats off to Capcom for delivering such an excellent Resident Evil game. I hope they become even more ambitious in the future. I’ll keep paying.

Just adding my voice to the choir. You already know if you want this game.  Although the Ethan Winters storyline helped to revitalize a flagging franchise, I was happy that Capcom chose to set it aside. Leon Kennedy has always been the star of my favorite Resident Evil games, and Requiem is no exception. I'm not an overly sentimental person, yet I found myself strangely emotional when confronted with an aging Leon.  Grace's sections bring the horror. They're not much different from RE7 and RE8. Maybe watered down a bit. Stalkers are present, but they patrol confined areas and are easily avoided. All of Grace's gameplay sections are indoors, and there aren't many puzzles. Most of the tension comes from an emphasis on resource management. I wasn't replenishing my ammo supply often enough and managed to softlock myself at one point.  Grace also brings the spectacle. Almost all story beats play out from her perspective, and this helps to compensate for any shortcomings in her gameplay.  Leon's sections bring the action. It's very satisfying to mow through the same enemies that have been causing Grace so much grief. I suppose you could say Leon has more puzzles. You have to find, combine, and use items to progress. Nothing requires logic. I think the game needs one more Grace interlude while Leon [spoiler]is in Raccoon City[/spoiler]. That section drags on too long, and sometimes crosses over into levels of ridiculousness that should be reserved for Chris Redfield.  Overall, I feel like Requiem has finally made good on the promise of RE6 -- a cast of playable characters with differing gameplay mechanics to highlight all of the strengths of a franchise straddling 2 genres. Overall Rating: 7/10  I think this is a solid entry in the Resident Evil franchise that brings back a lot of the best elements from previous entries with the two main character mechanic. Having Grace work as a first person stealth horror game (especially on Classic difficulty which I highly recommend) while Leon gets to kick ass is a perfect balance of the two kinds of gameplay the franchise is now known for. Grace feels very weak in an at-times genuinely scary way, and I think they did a great job making Leon's combat feel weighty and brutal, but still precise. I do think some of the Leon sections feel a little sluggish towards the end, but I have always been biased against that kind of gameplay which I know some others really like (i.e. big fans of RE4-RE6). The story here is as convoluted as other entries but it doesn't bog down the emotional moments too much, and there are enough mechanical flourishes tossed in throughout to keep the combat and stealth feeling fresh and exciting. I will say that I think the first half of the game feels a little stronger, because as things are revealed the story doesn't fully capitalize on the tone set up in that first act. But it isn't enough to drag the whole experience down, and I still appreciated the (somewhat egregious) fanservice that happens later on in the game. I hope they take this entry as a starting point for future games in the franchise and continue to work on melding stealth and action-adventure gameplay like this.

Resident Evil Requiem is a solid entry to the series. I wouldn't say the best, but it's a pretty great all-around experience.   The game is separated into 2 playstyles: Grace and Leon. Grace's sections are classic survival horror, more precisely the type of first-person survival horror Capcom developed with RE7, but with the foresight of that game in mind. Leon's sections are more action-horror oriented, very similarly to the RE4 remake.   Both are fun, but as a survival horror purist and big fan of the first 2 entries of the RE series, I vastly prefer the Grace sections. Every move you make feels methodical, the gameplay pace slows down, and you feel the need to experiment with how you play the game. What weapon should I use? Do I heal now? Should I go back and get this? Should I even use a weapon at all? This is what makes the early games, along with 7, so challenging but rewarding to play. All this to say that the early Grace sections in and under the care center are probably the best parts of the game. It's some of the best Resident Evil ever.   I don't hate the Leon sections, though. Resident Evil 4 is probably in the top 3 for me, but that's because of how well-crafted that game is. It's all this more action-oriented approach that's less horrifying than the games before it, but definitely still scary, with the added bonus of being genuinely a ton of fun. With Requiem, the swaps between styles mostly work, but you'll soon realize that the Leon sections feel somewhat less thought-out. I liked the Raccon City bits, but that one area with the tent felt especially drawn out and kinda dull in all honesty. It doesn't help that the environment is a lot more dull too, with lore reasons, but still. At least there's the lab at the end to sort of bring things back. And bring back the final Grace section that's arguably too short.  Story is serviceable, making connections with previous entries and expanding with Grace. It's nothing crazy, but the story is the envelope for the gameplay in these games. I would say all survival horror, but Silent Hill exists. For the next game, I hope they stick to one gameplay style, to be honest. I completed this in 15 hours, and 7.5 hours of each respective gameplay felt a bit short, even if I'm not typically a good game = longer game sort of person at all. My dream would be that an RE10 would be a first-person game. But I know action makes seemingly more money for Capcom. Still happy I chose to start playing Resident Evil remake 4 years ago.

Resident Evil 9 is something of a loveletter to the long-time fans of this venerable franchise. It's a highly polished, well-crafted package of pure, unashamed fan service and, as someone who's been with the series from the first game, it left me with a huge grin on my face the entire time.  The game perfectly balances the all-out cheesy action of 4-6 with the genuine dread and terror offered up by games like RE 2 and 7, switching between the perspectives of series newcomer Grace and grizzled veteran Leon S. Kennedy. Grace, rightfully so, is terrified the entire time and her sections rely on classic Resident Evil sneaking, resource management, map backtracking and light puzzle-solving to survive. Leon, meanwhile, has been here before. He's seen it all and he's an absolute tank of a man, destroying hordes of zombies with enough guns and one-liners to go toe-to-toe with any 80s action hero.  Although not quite as refined as RE4 Remake's incredibly well-tuned combat sandbox, there's an extremely satisfying weight to Leon's attacks and movement. He's older and feels slightly slower but far more hard-hitting.  Guns are extremely meaty with excellent audio-visual feedback and melee attacks are slow, purposeful and create a real sense of connection and power.  Grace, meanwhile, has far more limits imposed on her to heighten the fear factor. Her shots take longer to line up, her movement speed is slow, she's fragile, she has to scavenge for pretty scarce resources on higher difficulties. We all know at this point that Capcom are masters of tension and release survival horror, terrifying you before lulling into a sense of safety as you feel yourself mastering the challenge, only to hit you with new scares and surprises.  Grace's sections very much feel like that formula has been honed to its sharpest edge yet.  The story has proven pretty divisive, largely because of the sharp turn from personal stakes and trauma in the first half to grand conspiracies and classic supervillains in the latter half. I understand how this change in tone could be jarring, but personally I felt the rapidly escalating stakes of the main plot still did a fantastic job of centring the protagonists' personal journeys at their heart. Grace is haunted by trauma and self-blame, and by finding the courage to take these huge events head-on she begins the process of healing and self-forgiveness. Leon, under all the confidence is a man wracked with guilt and sorrow over the lives he couldn't save. In confronting the ghosts of the past and helping Grace, he finally achieves some sense of closure.   This is the most human Resident Evil game I've played.  The human cost, both to the two leads and the countless lives destroyed by greed and hubris in the series, is always front and centre. The game deals with the way the mistakes of the past still haunt us and how we can only move on if we dare to believe in hope. For me, although you might be able to find some individual flaws in the plotting of the game, this thematic backbone is handled wonderfully and makes for a Resident Evil game that genuinely provoked some introspection and feels.  I won't go as far as to say this is the best of the series. For me that will always be a tie between the first game, RE2 remake and RE4 remake. But Requiem easily takes pride of place among the greats of the franchise and delivers everything you want; nostalgia, genuine horror, tightly-crafted action setpieces and a deeply human story about loss and the mistakes of the past.  Capcom have done it again.   9/10

Just off of my first playthrough vibes in Classic mode, where saving as Grace requires ink ribbons. For reference, the only other RE game I've personally played is RE4 Re.  I think this game is a beautiful amalgamation of the gameplay concepts Capcom has introduced in the Resident Evil series. We went from, early on, horror-based stealth and resource management gameplay, to more run-and-gun gameplay midway through the series, then looped back to said horror-based stealth gameplay in the more recent installments.   This game mixes the both, but specifically by making you play out two different storylines at the same time. You get the slow paced, careful, and stealth-based gameplay of Grace, and the fast, guns-blazing gameplay with Leon. I greatly enjoyed both, being able to relive the badassery of Leon and the slow burn horror of Grace. Notably, I'm terrible with horror games, but the limited amount of agency you get as Grace greatly helped balancing the experience.   Grace's section is amazing. The horror elements, extremely limited resources, and first-person immersion made for extremely tense gameplay. The ink ribbon shortage mainly came from balancing crafting those versus consumables. I didn't really experience a *problem* with the lack of ink ribbons, but if you aren't crafting a bunch, you can come really close to running out of them.  Leon's section is very fun, but admittedly a smidge lackluster. I miss the unique quirks of each weapon that you unlock when you max-upgrade them. The customizability of your build is lacking in this regard. The guns do feel good to use, but I wish we got more of them.   Additionally, Leon's movement feels very momentum-heavy. When running, sharp movements are always accompanied by some of your initial momentum. Takes getting used to, and feels a little less responsive, but that may just be the intended gameplay experience.  The resource management is... as usual. There are no Red or Yellow herbs, but outside of that, most things are par for the course. I do believe that my exploration efforts were insufficient to find attachments, as I barely found any, but I don't know for sure that I missed a bunch of them. Thus, you don't really tend to find many permanent upgrades, which felt... weird, to me. Purchased, yes, but found, not really.  Overall, it's peak, 9/10. Will go back and play Insane mode(with Grace's section in 3rd person, I'm too much of a baby).

RE9 feels like a game that’s constantly borrowing from better entries in the series without really understanding what made them work. The setup has potential, but it quickly falls into a loop of predictable story beats, paper-thin characters, and twists that feel telegraphed long before they happen. By the time the game tries to surprise you, it’s already too late—you’ve seen it all coming.  The gameplay is competent but never exciting. Combat works, exploration is serviceable, and the pacing is decent enough, but nothing stands out. It leans heavily on familiar mechanics without adding anything meaningful, so it ends up feeling more like going through the motions than actually surviving a horror experience. Even the set pieces, which should be highlights, feel recycled and oddly safe.  What really drags it down is the lack of identity. It doesn’t commit fully to horror, action, or psychological tension—instead it awkwardly sits in the middle, never pushing far enough in any direction to be memorable. The atmosphere has its moments, but they’re fleeting and often undercut by cliché dialogue and predictable encounters.  It’s not a bad game by any means—it runs well, looks decent, and fans will probably find some enjoyment in the familiarity. But that’s also the problem: it relies too much on that familiarity. In the end, RE9 is the definition of average—a polished but uninspired entry that plays it safe at every turn and leaves very little lasting impression once you’re done.
